acting in a clandestine fashion When they were married together in Lisbon Primarily to thwart the Inquisition Which eventually did make its way to Portugal But they underwrote a lot of activities To try and prevent the Church From extending the Inquisition there Including very liberal bribes And perhaps even some assassinations Of Inquisitorial officials But the Inquisition was impossible to hold back And the smallest thing could set them off So for example There was in the Jewish Quarter Of Lisbon Which they still had Like a Jewish Quarter Kind of a ghetto type of setup But it was more like What they would call in Boca Raton A gated community There was a young Christian courtier Who was seeking out a young Jewish woman That he had met in the marketplace Earlier that day And he went into a house Hoping to find her And he discovered a whole bunch of Jews Gathered there around the table And this happened to be Erev Pesach The Passover Seder And of course These are new Christians Conversos And of course He came out And he proclaimed this in the streets And it caused quite a hue and cry Similarly in another occasion When there was a plague raging in the city A whole bunch of new Christians And older Christians Were gathered in a church And they were praying for redemption From this plague And the light shining through The windows in the back Lit up a cross at one end of the room With an unusual luminescence Many of the Christians in the room Felt that this was a miraculous sign That in fact The plague was about to be lifted And a converso You can tell it's kind of a Jewish approach He scoffed at the idea That this trick of the light Meant there was divine favor This incensed the entire church population And a riot ensued shortly thereafter So you can see the kind of tinderbox That Lisbon was at the time As the inquisition was approaching So she decided to flee Lisbon And make her way to Antwerp Where her surviving brother-in-law Was living and making business Tremendous difficulty getting out Of any of the places she tried to get out Because of course her phenomenal wealth Meant that the ruling authorities Refused to allow her passage On the one hand They didn't want to insult her Because they wanted to keep her wealth intact And keep her working for the benefit Of the larger economy And so they couldn't simply refuse her passage She is allowed to travel But on the other hand If they allow her to travel There's always the worry That she would not come back And that is in fact what she did She made her way up to London Where there was a kind of a Secret underground railway For Marranos For those who wanted to flee Out of Spain and Portugal And then from there she went Across the English Channel To Antwerp where she met up with her brother She brought with her a character That I have not mentioned yet But someone who will be very important In her later life Her younger sister Brianda And Brianda who would later marry Diogo Would eventually have a child Her younger sister as we shall see Did not share Gracia's attitude towards Judaism And in fact this would have disastrous Consequences for all of them Later on just to jump ahead of our story Because we have this beautiful map here She made her way down to the south of France To Venice for a while To Ferrara where she was very active And she most likely It is in Ferrara where she finally Renounced her Christian status And returned to Judaism And eventually she made her way To Constantinople where she Most likely passed away Constantinople at this time Was of course ruled by the Ottoman Turks Who were Muslims Who were openly inviting Jews To come to Muslim lands And were laughing out loud In print and in all kinds of proclamations That the Christian persecution of Jews Was in fact enriching the Ottoman territories Very famous passages from Various sultans to this effect When she was in Ferrara And particularly recall at this point She met up with Diogo And there is a lot of fascinating Sort of behind the scenes negotiations Over the will, the estate That belonged to her late husband And her brother Ultimately her brother-in-law Ceded her complete control Over the entire wealth Of the house of Nasi Even over his own wife and daughter He felt that she would be A much better steward of that wealth Than his wife As we shall see for good reason So when she was in Ferrara Up until this point They've been extremely generous In fundraising And in producing resources For Jews who are fleeing persecution And actively promoting The rescue of conversos In particular from various Persecutions And depredations at the hand of the church In Ferrara she's able to Spend her money a little differently And she becomes a great patron Of Jewish scholarship Two works in particular Are associated with her activity The first is The work of Samuel Ouske A famous work which Has been translated to English The Consolations for the Tribulations of Israel Which is a sort of historical And a philosophical work About the nature of Jewish Persecution over the centuries And then the famous Ferrara Bible Which is a translation Of the Hebrew Tanakh Into Judeo-Spanish Into Ladino And it's got a fascinating kind of cover on it You can see that the frontispiece Has a depiction of a ship In a stormy sea With sea monsters And a broken mast And it's an unusual kind of emblem To put on the front page Of a Bible Does anyone have any thoughts Why she would choose to have it decorated so? This special Bible Written in the spirit really of the age With Luther publishing in German And so on Writing a Bible that conversos could read In a language that they were Trained in, schooled in And yet having this kind of image on the cover What do you think about The experience of the Jews as a whole? Can you imagine these conversos Travelling from place to place Trying to stay afloat And yet the mast is broken And the winds are blowing I like the wind over here in the corner It's very dangerous And nevertheless they're making their way Through the sea I find it a very evocative and beautiful image myself Okay, well let's go on I find that fascinating Now at this point, family conflict So let's recall That the way the wealth is managed Up until this point She has all the money from her Husband and Diogo Her brother-in-law in Antwerp Has the other half That's largely because Her husband felt that Diogo had Assisted in producing that wealth But in reality it was her husband Who made most of it At any rate, when she gets to Antwerp She becomes right away Diogo's Right hand person Diogo ends up marrying her Younger sister And having a child Who is known as La Chica Beatrice, after her aunt After Gracia La Chica means the young one And that's often used to distinguish her from her aunt But It seems that Her sister, younger sister Is really not enthusiastic About all the schlepping around And the secret converso Culture stuff She was really happy in Lisbon She was happy living as a Christian And All this, you know On the razor's edge Worried about what's going to happen to the family What's going to happen to our money Do we really, are you actually seriously Talking about moving to Istanbul Of all places It didn't appeal to her at all And she becomes more and more Restive when it comes to the Discussions that her husband And Gracia were having About the possibility of fleeing Europe Altogether Ultimately, after Diogo passes away And in his will, as I mentioned earlier All the money in the control of Gracia, his sister-in-law Not his wife and his daughter Gracia The younger daughter The younger sister, Brianda Would formally denounce her own sister To the church And claim that Her sister, truthfully Her sister was secretly living As a Jew And that she, therefore, Brianda The younger sister Deserved all of the wealth Of the family And her sister should be arrested Possibly tortured and killed And so on It was a really difficult point in Gracia's life If you can imagine This human conflict had reached such a Fever pitch But it was clear there was no turning back Between the two of them The idea of fleeing Europe altogether And living in a Muslim country Was something that was so foreign To Brianda's way of thinking She had grown used to the Life of heavy consumption That was associated with the Uber wealthy of Europe And she simply would have nothing of it She plied her Now, Gracia had anticipated this And had very liberally Greased the palms Of all kinds of church And temporal officials Trying to hold back a formal lawsuit Challenging her authority She was not able to Prevent a lawsuit from actually Reaching the court, but she was Extremely able to defeat Her sister in legal battle And lay authoritative claim To the entire inheritance Which was a rather amazing feat And it just shows you How useful money is On the other hand In a related development There was also a rabbinic court Convened on This particular issue That included some of the greatest minds Of the era Don't forget this is the 16th century Era when you have Moshe Ditrani for example And you have none other than Rav Yosef Karo, the author Of the Code of Jewish Law, the Shulchan Orach Who debated this very point And ironically The author of the Shulchan Orach, Yosef Karo Disagreed with Gracia Mendez Even though he felt that she was A wonderful person and they did great things For the Jewish people and so on It wasn't right that the sister Didn't get an inheritance and that The niece didn't get an inheritance either And that's another story beyond What we're going to discuss here Part of this whole debate Was surrounding as well Who would the younger child marry Who would Beatrice La Chica end up marrying One of the And at this point I've kind of omitted discussion Of the role of kings here But there was tremendous involvement Of kings and queens All having designs on the money Of the House of Nasi In this particular case The younger sister had a wife Who wanted to marry off La Chica to one of her closest friends And in so doing Hope to garner A large section of the assets That belonged to the Nasi family When the queen approached Gracia Nasi about this She actually avoided her Several times by feigning illness And when was finally forced To answer up front What would she say about This particular marriage To her niece To this older Christian man Gracia Nasi said Intemperately I'd rather see my niece drowned Than married to that man Very strong language Which meant she really had to flee Europe Because there was no more Excuse for her at that point So they ended up finally Making their way to Istanbul And at this point Gracia Nasi had revealed Her Jewish identity And she had no Jewish causes Without any Vacillation or dissimulation But she met with several setbacks One that's very important Is the Altona incident Of 1556 Which was perhaps the saddest moment In her career There was an Italian city With a port called Ancona And they had a very zealous Inquisitor there Sent by a new pope Paul IV And a very large Converso community And these are Remember what are we talking about here We would have in Ancona We had the regular Jews The Italian Jews who had lived there since time immemorial Who were not forced to convert to Christianity You had regular Christians And then you had this converso community Largely made up of Portuguese Jews Who were formally converted to Christianity And were In such confession But were nevertheless Pretty much openly as Jews Marrying with each other, keeping kosher And all kinds of things like this And they could not Declare themselves openly To be Jewish Because that would be in contravention of church law You can't simply convert to Christianity And then convert back again But they were not prepared To live as Christians So you had these three distinct populations In Ancona as you did in many Centers where Jews settled The pope and his Religious inquisitor Arrested approximately a hundred Of these conversos in Ancona And proceeded to Take the traditional Inquisitorial route of Torturing them Extracting confessions Arresting others and so on And threatening to burn them Gracia Mendes of course was incensed And wanted to do everything possible To prevent the abuse Of her co-religionists But she was unable To succeed She actually went so far as to enlist the aid Of the Sultan of Turkey Which she had that level of contact with And the Sultan sent an emissary To Ancona To indicate that any sort of Maltreatment of these conversos Would result in potentially Military action From the Ottoman Empire Gracia also rounded up A huge number of Jewish communities Who agreed to Impose a boycott On the port of Ancona And to bring that city to its knees Economically Because Jews were extremely involved In all kinds of international trade And refusing to do business With that particular port Would actually bring their trade To a standstill Unfortunately she was unable To achieve unanimity On the question of a boycott There were a few holdouts Notably the Italian Jews Of Ancona Who felt that they were being unfairly Drawn into this international dispute There were not always Friendly relations Between traditional Jews And conversos They were living in very distinct communities Even though they had quite a bit Of relations with each other They were certainly not into marrying So they felt that they were going to have Their livelihoods destroyed by this boycott And they argued against it As did several local communities Who were heavily dependent on the Ancona trade And so despite her tremendous efforts She was not able to bring together The Judaism Jewry with one voice On this issue and the boycott failed And 100 Jews Were put to death As a result of the inquisitorial flames She however Devoted most of the energies Of the last years of her life To developing the land of Israel With some very fascinating projects One of them most famously Is the city of Tiberia Or Tiberias Which she essentially bought From the Ottoman Turks She received an exclusive grant In perpetuity To develop The city of Tiberias On the Sea of Galilee In exchange of course For funds that would be produced And would be given to the Ottoman Turks On a regular basis So the very city of Tiberia Which is modeled in many ways on the successful city of Tiberias Nearby is a result of Doña Gracia's specific intervention And her philanthropy So if we want to bring it back To look at her legacy This is perhaps our best chance Of guessing what she actually looked like This is a medallion That was struck In honor of her Nieces 18th birthday And you can see That it says in Hebrew Gracia Nasi On her 18th birthday This is the niece Known as La Chica So to whatever degree there is A family resemblance That's the degree to which we can get a sense Of how our Heroine actually looked The medallion was most likely Struck on the occasion Of her marriage To Don Joseph Nasi Also a family member But the overall Scope and trajectory we get Of the life of this really Phenomenal woman is one of Unrelenting heroism And one of an indomitable Will in which she's Confronted with these very difficult challenges The challenges of great wealth The challenge of Jewish identity Within a very hostile environment And throughout it all she Maintains a very steadfast Support of the Jewish people She allows her Burning love for Judaism To Remain within her soul For the vast majority of Her life while she is outwardly Practicing as a Christian and only When she is finally free to express herself As a Jew does she ultimately Reveal her full intent But we see her impact on the Jewish World in so many ways Not only in the land of Israel but also In the overall legacy of the Jewish People as a whole I want to thank you very much for your intention And your endurance tonight And I hope you have a fantastic week We're going to come back to speak About another somewhat more tragic Figure from the Spanish and Portuguese experience Thank you Stand clear of the closing doors please

title: Could You Patent the Sun? The Polio Vaccine Salk Never Owned
text: On April 12, 1955, in a packed auditorium in Ann Arbor, Michigan, a scientist stepped to a microphone and told a frightened nation that the polio vaccine worked safe, effective, potent. Within hours, church bells rang and factories paused. That evening, the broadcaster Edward R. Murrow put one question to the man who made it, Jonas Salk, who owns the patent on this vaccine, and Salk gave the answer that would outlive him by decades. Well, the people, I would say, there is no patent. Could you patent the sun? It is the most famous refusal in the history of invention. And almost no one knows the part that complicates it. Start with what there was to own. Polio paralyzed and killed thousands of children every year, and the fear of it shut swimming pools and emptied summers. Salk's vaccine used a killed virus, poliovirus-grown, inactivated, and injected to teach the body to defend itself without causing the disease. To grow that virus in quantity, Salk relied on a method he did not invent a way of culturing poliovirus in ordinary, non-nervous tissues. That method had been published by John Enders, Thomas Weller, and Frederick Robbins. And in 1954, the year before Salk's triumph, it won them the Nobel Prize. That detail is the whole case. Because a patent protects what is new and non-obvious. And the foundational step that made the vaccine possible was already in the literature, already credited, already public. So when we ask what Salk could have claimed, the honest answer is less than the legend suggests. The vaccine was a magnificent assembly of work that was, in large part, already known. Here is the part the famous quote leaves out. Before Murrow ever asked his question, lawyers for the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, the March of Dimes, the charity that had funded all of it, had already studied whether the vaccine could be patented. The biographer, Jane Smith, found the documents in the foundation's own archives. The conclusion was not romantic. It was technical. The vaccine did not meet the novelty requirement, an application the attorneys judged would fail. One patent lawyer's assessment survives, almost word for word, if there was any patentable novelty to be found, it would lie within an extremely narrow scope and would be of doubtful value. Read that twice, doubtful value. The foundation was not weighing a fortune and nobly declining it. Its own counsel had concluded there was likely no enforceable patent to file in the first place. Because of the prior art, because of Enders, because the science underneath was shared. And there is a second layer. The money was never really Salk's to capture. The research, the labs, the 1950 for-field trial across roughly 1.8 million children, all of it was paid for by the public. Dimes mailed in by ordinary Americans through a charity. By 1955, the effort had absorbed tens of millions of dollars and donated money. The invention had been publicly funded from the start. In a real sense, it already belonged to the people before Salk ever said so on television. So what was actually resolved here? Not a lawsuit, not a verdict. There was no courtroom. Because there was nothing to litigate. And that is the ruling. The system that decides who owns an invention reached its conclusion before any judge could the patent office would not have granted a meaningful claim. The famous line, could you patent the sun, describes a legal fact as much as a moral one. You cannot patent something built openly on published, credited prior work. The sun in this metaphor is prior art. And the world saw almost immediately what a noun looked like in practice. Within weeks of the announcement, drug companies were mass producing the vaccine. There was no licensor controlling quality, no single owner holding the keys. That openness had a cost. In April 1955, defective lots from one maker, Cutter Laboratories, contained live virus that had not been fully killed. By the accounts that followed, tens of thousands of children were exposed. Hundreds were paralyzed and 10 died. The disaster forced the United States to rebuild how it regulates vaccines. It is the dark companion to the gift a thing owned by everyone is also in the rush. Controlled by no one. So who won and who lost? Salk became a secular saint and stayed by choice a salaried scientist. He never grew rich from the vaccine. Decades later, one estimate guessed he had walked away from something like seven billion dollars. Treat that as a later thought experiment. Not a number anyone offered him in 1955. The patent his foundation studied was judged to be of doubtful value at the time. By 1961, Albert Sabin's live oral vaccine had arrived and would largely replace Salk's injection for a generation, which complicates even the claim that Salk's specific design won. What endured was not a fortune or a monopoly. What endured was the sentence. Could you patent the sun became the rallying cry for everyone who argues that some inventions are too important to own. Quoted in every fight over the price of medicine since. The irony the cry forgets Salk's vaccine may have been unpatentable on the merits. The most celebrated act of giving an invention away may have been, in part, a man gracefully accepting what the law, had already decided. That is the lesson of this file. And it cuts against the easy version. In file one, Robert Kearns held an airtight patent and spent 17 years proving the world owed him for it. Ownership that bought him nothing but a fight. Here, Salk held no patent at all, captured none of the money and became a mortal. Owning the invention destroyed one man. Giving it away or never being able to keep it made the other a legend. The patent system rewards the claim, not the contribution. And the two come apart far more often than we admit. Next time's an inventor who handed the world a technology on purpose, wrote it into the open and watched an entire industry get rich on the thing he refused to lock up.
